CHAPTER 4: EVIDENCE FOR JESUS OF NAZARETH (Section B: Christianity - Origins and Contemporary Expressions)

BIG IDEA
- How do we know about Jesus? There are two kinds of evidence: secular (non-religious) evidence from Roman and Jewish historians, and the gospels (religious, faith documents).
- There are no primary sources for the life of Jesus, but this is normal for ancient history.
- The gospels are our principal source. They are "faith documents" written between 70 and 100 CE, and must be read in context.
- Opening quote, Luke 1:1-4: Luke writes "an orderly account" for "most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth concerning the things about which you have been instructed", based on what was handed on by "eyewitnesses and servants of the word".

KEY TERMS
- Secular: non-religious (as distinct from religious). Secular evidence for Jesus comes from Roman and Jewish historians.
- Primary source: an original document giving direct evidence of an event, e.g. a manuscript of a speech, a diary by a contemporary, newspaper accounts of the time.
- Secondary source: a source written later, at a remove from the person or event; the writer may have used primary sources.
- Authoritative source: a source that can be trusted and relied on as reliable evidence.
- Synoptic gospels: Matthew, Mark and Luke - "synoptic" means written from a common perspective.
- Evangelists: the writers of the gospels (from the Greek euangelion).
- Gospel: from the Greek euangelion, meaning "good news".
- Q: a theory of a lost source of sayings and incidents shared by Matthew and Luke but not in Mark.
- Oral tradition: passing on the faith by word of mouth.

INTRODUCTION - HOW WILL FUTURE GENERATIONS KNOW?
- Example: 11 September 2001 - the bombing of the World Trade Centre and the Pentagon and loss of life in three air crashes.
- In a hundred years almost everyone alive then will be dead; future generations will rely on sources.
- This raises the question of how we learn about Jesus.

JESUS IN HISTORY
- We usually turn to historians to understand the past.
- For thousands of years people recorded important events through drawings, stories, songs, poetry and writing.
- It is human nature to want to understand our past.
- Roman historians made only a few references to Jesus. They were preoccupied with Rome and the Empire and had little interest in events far from Rome, which only affected Rome after Jesus' death.
- Secular evidence comes from two Roman historians: Pliny the Younger (writing around 111 CE) and Tacitus (writing around 115 CE). Also the Jewish historian Josephus.

PLINY THE YOUNGER (61-113 CE)
- Governor of a Roman province in Asia Minor.
- Wrote to Emperor Trajan asking advice on what to do with the Christians in his province.
- Roman governors worried about any group that might cause a disturbance.
- Mentions Jesus in this context but gives no extra information about him.

TACITUS (c. 56-117 CE)
- Roman historian.
- Referred to Jesus when writing about the burning of Rome in 64 CE.
- Emperor Nero blamed the Christians for the fire, though many historians think Nero himself may have been responsible.
- Tacitus had no time for Christians. Quote: "Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of... Pontius Pilate, and the pernicious superstition [Christianity] was checked for a moment, only to break out once more, not merely in Judea, the home of the disease, but in the capital [Rome] itself..."
- He describes Nero's brutal treatment of Christians: "Christians were covered with wild beasts' skins and torn to death by dogs; or they were fastened on crosses and, when daylight failed, were burned to serve as lamps by night." (Not all historians accept this claim.)
- Tacitus was a hostile reporter of Jesus and the Christian movement.
- His evidence confirms: Jesus (Christus) existed, was executed under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius, and Christianity spread from Judea to Rome.

JOSEPHUS (FLAVIUS JOSEPHUS) (c. 37-100 CE)
- A Jewish historian; mentions Jesus more favourably.
- Wrote several books of Jewish history, including The Jewish War (seven volumes) and The Jewish Antiquities (twenty volumes).
- Defended Galilee against Rome in the great Jewish rebellion; surrendered after his forces were overrun by Emperor Vespasian in 66 CE.
- Joined the entourage of Vespasian in Rome and later of Emperor Titus (Vespasian's eldest son), so took their family name, Flavius.
- Mentioned Jesus near the end of his life, about sixty years after the crucifixion.
- Jesus is mentioned in the context of disturbances by Jews in the reign of Pontius Pilate (26-36 CE); Josephus saw Jesus as central to these.
- Describes Jesus as "a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure."
- Josephus accepted both the historical reality of Jesus and that he had a profound and lasting impact on the people he met.

EVALUATING THE SECULAR EVIDENCE
- All these sources give evidence for the historical reality of Jesus and primary evidence for the spread and impact of Christianity.
- They must be considered authoritative because of the (somewhat hostile) nature of the witnesses - they had no reason to invent Jesus.

PRIMARY AND SECONDARY SOURCES
- Primary source: original document, direct evidence (speech manuscript, contemporary diary, newspaper of the time).
- In this sense there are no primary sources for the life of Jesus.
- This is not unusual for ancient history - there are no primary sources for the life of Socrates either.
- The gospels do reflect some history, e.g. the fact that Jesus spoke Aramaic.
- Secondary source: written later, at a remove; has information about the period; writer may have used primary sources.

ARE THE GOSPELS BIOGRAPHIES?
- The gospels are believed to be an authoritative source about Jesus; they are historical to a certain degree.
- Scholars debate whether they are biographies.
- They are "lives" of Jesus in the sense normal for the Greco-Roman world (milieu) of the time - remarkably similar to other biographies of their time.
- They do not match our modern idea of biography - e.g. they tell nothing about Jesus' life from age twelve to thirty.
- Christians believe them to be the inspired word of God, so they are authoritative.

THE GOSPELS AS SOURCES
- Our principal source for the life and vision of Jesus.
- New Testament documents written between 70 and 100 CE.
- "Difficulties": written after Jesus' death, one a century after his birth; written by people who believed in the resurrection and saw Jesus as the risen Lord - this faith influenced how and what they wrote.
- Each was written at a particular time, place and for a particular group - reading them with this in mind is examining the gospels "in context".
- Being "faith documents" does not weaken them as sources. Jesus inspired faith in himself and his mission; the gospels as reflections of faith give rich insight into the man and his mission.
- Context (target audience, political situation, background of the writer) can influence any historical document.

THE SYNOPTIC GOSPELS AND Q
- The writers are the evangelists.
- Matthew, Mark and Luke are the synoptic gospels - written from a common perspective.
- Scholars believe Matthew and Luke used the earlier gospel of Mark.
- Matthew and Luke also share a large body of sayings and incidents not found in Mark.
- Scholars propose another source they both used, called "Q". No written copy of Q exists; it is a theory that helps explain the similarities and differences between the synoptics.
- John's gospel is quite different: its writer did not use Q or the earlier gospels but drew on eyewitness accounts and other sources.
- Assignment comparison: birth of Jesus in Matthew 2:1-15 and Luke 2:1-20.

THE THREE PHASES OF GOSPEL FORMATION (each roughly thirty years; approximate)
- Phase 1: the life, ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth.
- Phase 2: the period before the gospels were written - the early disciples preached and taught about Jesus and came to understand his mission more fully (oral tradition).
- Phase 3: the compilation of the gospels - four people in four different places recorded the mission and message of Jesus in writing.
- So the gospels cannot simply be read as four biographies.
- The early Church depended largely on the oral tradition; disciples had to remember the sayings and deeds of their master. Gospels were written only when it became necessary and culturally appropriate.

PAUL'S LETTERS
- Before the gospels, Paul wrote about the life, death and resurrection of Jesus to help his newly founded Christian communities, answering questions and giving guidance.
- 1 Thessalonians 4:1-2: "...as you learned from us how you ought to live and to please God... you should do so more and more. For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus."
- He encouraged followers to live as Jesus did.
- Other writers at this time recorded stories, parables and eyewitness accounts of Jesus.
- Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians was written between 49 and 51 CE (generally agreed) - earlier than the gospels.

ONE GOSPEL
- The New Testament has four documents called gospels, but there is only one Gospel - the gospel of and about Jesus Christ.
- English "gospel" comes from Greek euangelion = "good news"; "evangelist" comes from the same word.
- Paul used "euangelion" for the message proclaimed by the apostles and himself (see 2 Timothy 2:8).

KEY DATES SUMMARY
- Pontius Pilate's rule: 26-36 CE.
- Paul's 1 Thessalonians: 49-51 CE.
- Burning of Rome: 64 CE.
- Vespasian overruns Josephus' forces: 66 CE.
- Gospels written: 70-100 CE.
- Pliny writes: around 111 CE. Tacitus writes: around 115 CE.

rows.prompt: What are the key points in the secular evidence about Jesus?
rows.model_answer: Pliny the Younger wrote to Emperor Trajan about Christians in his province. Tacitus said Christus was executed by Pontius Pilate in Tiberius' reign and that Christianity spread to Rome. Josephus called Jesus a wise man and doer of wonderful works who had a lasting impact.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a primary and a secondary source.
rows.model_answer: A primary source is an original document that gives direct evidence of an event, like a diary or newspaper of the time. A secondary source is written later, at a remove from the event, and its writer may have used primary sources.

rows.prompt: Explain why Tacitus is described as a 'hostile' witness.
rows.model_answer: Tacitus had no time for Christians and called Christianity a 'pernicious superstition' and a 'disease'. Yet he still recorded that Christus was executed by Pontius Pilate. Because he was against Christianity, he had no reason to invent Jesus, which makes his evidence more authoritative.

rows.prompt: Why does being a 'faith document' not weaken the gospels as sources?
rows.model_answer: The gospels were written by believers in the risen Lord, and this faith shaped what they wrote. But Jesus inspired faith in himself and his mission, so the gospels as reflections of that faith give a rich insight into both the man and his mission.

rows.prompt: Name two 'difficulties' in using the gospels as historical sources.
rows.model_answer: They were written after Jesus' death, between 70 and 100 CE, one of them a century after his birth. They were written by people who believed in the resurrection, and this faith influenced how and what they wrote. Each was also written for a particular time, place and group.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by the 'synoptic gospels' and the 'Q' source.
rows.model_answer: Matthew, Mark and Luke are the synoptic gospels, written from a common perspective; Matthew and Luke used Mark. They also share material not in Mark, so scholars suggest they used another source called Q. No copy of Q exists; it is a theory.

rows.prompt: Outline the three phases in the formation of the gospels.
rows.model_answer: Phase 1 was the life, ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus. Phase 2 was the period when the disciples preached and taught about Jesus by word of mouth. Phase 3 was when four people in four places wrote the gospels down. Each phase was roughly thirty years.

rows.prompt: Why did Paul write letters, and how do they relate to the gospels?
rows.model_answer: Paul wrote to his newly founded Christian communities to answer questions and give guidance, encouraging them to live as Jesus did. His first letter to the Thessalonians was written around 49-51 CE, so his letters were written before the gospels.

rows.prompt: Outline the evidence for Jesus of Nazareth found in the writings of two non-Christian historians.
rows.model_answer:
Tacitus (c. 56-117 CE) was a Roman historian writing around 115 CE. He referred to Jesus when writing about the burning of Rome in 64 CE, which Emperor Nero blamed on the Christians. Tacitus wrote that 'Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of... Pontius Pilate', and that this 'pernicious superstition' broke out again in Judea and in Rome itself. He was hostile to Christianity, yet he confirms that Jesus lived, was executed under Pilate, and that his movement spread.

Josephus (c. 37-100 CE) was a Jewish historian who wrote The Jewish War and The Jewish Antiquities. After surrendering to Vespasian he joined the emperor's entourage and took the name Flavius. About sixty years after the crucifixion he mentioned Jesus in the context of Jewish disturbances under Pontius Pilate (26-36 CE). He described Jesus as 'a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure'. Josephus accepted that Jesus was historically real and had a profound and lasting impact on those he met.

May refer to: Pliny the Younger (61-113 CE, governor in Asia Minor, letter to Trajan c. 111 CE about Christians); Tacitus (c. 56-117, burning of Rome 64 CE, Nero, Christus, Tiberius, Pilate, 'pernicious superstition', hostile); Josephus (c. 37-100, Jewish War, Antiquities, Flavius, 60 years after, 'wise man', impact).

rows.prompt: Evaluate the gospels as sources of information about Jesus of Nazareth, both as historical accounts and as 'faith documents'.
rows.model_answer:
The gospels are our principal source for the life and vision of Jesus. As historical accounts they have strengths and limits. There are no primary sources for Jesus' life, but this is normal in ancient history - there are none for Socrates either. The gospels clearly reflect some history, such as the fact that Jesus spoke Aramaic, and they are historical to a certain degree. They are 'lives' of Jesus typical of Greco-Roman biographies of their time, though not modern biographies, since they say nothing of Jesus' life from twelve to thirty.

However, they were written between 70 and 100 CE, after Jesus' death, following about thirty years of oral tradition in which the disciples preached and came to understand his mission. They were written for particular communities in particular places, so they must be read in context. Matthew and Luke used Mark and possibly a source called Q, while John drew on eyewitness accounts.

As faith documents, they were written by people who believed Jesus was the risen Lord, and this influenced how and what they wrote. But this does not weaken them. Jesus inspired faith in himself and his mission, so the gospels give rich insight into both the man and his mission. Christians also believe them to be the inspired word of God, which makes them authoritative.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Must address both historical and faith aspects. May refer to: no primary sources (Socrates); Aramaic; Greco-Roman 'lives'; gap 12-30; dated 70-100 CE; three phases; oral tradition; context (time, place, audience); synoptics, Mark, Q, John; written by believers in resurrection; faith gives insight; inspired word of God.

rows.prompt: Describe the three stages in the development of the gospels, and explain why the gospels cannot simply be read as four biographies.
rows.model_answer:
The emergence of the gospels can be divided into three approximate phases, each roughly thirty years long. Phase 1 was the life, ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth. Phase 2 was the period before the gospels were written. The early disciples preached and taught about Jesus, remembering the sayings and deeds of their master, and in the process came to understand his mission more fully. The early Church depended largely on this oral tradition. During this time Paul also wrote letters to his new communities, such as 1 Thessalonians (49-51 CE), and others recorded stories, parables and eyewitness accounts. Phase 3 was the compilation of the gospels, when four people in four different places recorded the message of Jesus in writing, between 70 and 100 CE. This happened only when it became necessary and culturally appropriate.

So the gospels cannot simply be read as biographies. They were shaped by decades of preaching and by the faith of their writers in the risen Lord, and each was written for a particular group at a particular time and place.
rows.marking_scheme: Three phases x 2 marks + explanation 4 marks. May refer to: Phase 1 life/death/resurrection; Phase 2 oral tradition, preaching, deeper understanding, Paul's letters; Phase 3 four writers, four places, 70-100 CE; roughly 30 years each; faith and context shape the text; written when necessary and culturally appropriate.

rows.prompt: Explain the relationship between the synoptic gospels and how John's gospel differs from them. Refer to the meaning of 'gospel' and 'evangelist' in your answer.
rows.model_answer:
The English word 'gospel' comes from the Greek euangelion, meaning 'good news'. The gospel writers are called evangelists, from the same word. Paul also used euangelion for the message proclaimed by the apostles and himself. Although the New Testament has four gospels, there is in fact only one Gospel - the gospel of and about Jesus Christ.

Matthew, Mark and Luke are known as the synoptic gospels, meaning they were written from a common perspective. Scripture scholars believe they are linked because Matthew and Luke used the earlier gospel of Mark when writing their own. Matthew and Luke also share a large body of sayings of Jesus and incidents not found in Mark. This led scholars to the theory of another source, called 'Q', to which both had access. No written copy of Q exists, so it remains a theory that helps explain the similarities and differences between the synoptic gospels. For example, the birth stories in Matthew 2:1-15 and Luke 2:1-20 can be compared.

John's gospel is quite different from the other three. Its writer did not use Q or the earlier gospels but drew on eyewitness accounts and other sources for the life of Jesus.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: euangelion = good news; evangelists; one Gospel; synoptic = common perspective; Matthew and Luke used Mark; shared non-Mark material; Q theory, no copy exists; John independent, eyewitness accounts; birth narratives comparison.
